claim: Ultradian (~4 hr) rhythms in locomotor activity that do not depend on the master circadian pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus have been observed across mammalian species.
source: Ultradian (∼4 hr) rhythms in locomotor activity that do not depend on the master circadian pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus have been observed across mammalian species, however, the underlying mechanisms driving these rhythms are unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing the existence of ultradian rhythms across species.

claim: The underlying mechanisms driving ultradian rhythms are unknown.
source: Ultradian (∼4 hr) rhythms in locomotor activity that do not depend on the master circadian pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus have been observed across mammalian species, however, the underlying mechanisms driving these rhythms are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Disruption of the dopamine transporter gene lengthens the period of ultradian locomotor rhythms in mice.
source: We show that disruption of the dopamine transporter gene lengthens the period of ultradian locomotor rhythms in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2 showing period lengthening in Slc6a3−/− mice.

claim: Period lengthening results from chemogenetic activation of midbrain dopamine neurons.
source: Period lengthening also results from chemogenetic activation of midbrain dopamine neurons and psychostimulant treatment, while the antipsychotic haloperidol has the opposite effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 8 showing period lengthening upon CNO treatment in AAV-hM3Dq transduced mice.

claim: Period lengthening results from psychostimulant treatment.
source: Period lengthening also results from chemogenetic activation of midbrain dopamine neurons and psychostimulant treatment, while the antipsychotic haloperidol has the opposite effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4 showing period lengthening with methamphetamine treatment.

claim: The antipsychotic haloperidol has the opposite effect on ultradian period compared to psychostimulants.
source: Period lengthening also results from chemogenetic activation of midbrain dopamine neurons and psychostimulant treatment, while the antipsychotic haloperidol has the opposite effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing period shortening with haloperidol treatment.

claim: Striatal dopamine levels fluctuate in synchrony with ultradian activity cycles.
source: We further reveal that striatal dopamine levels fluctuate in synchrony with ultradian activity cycles and that dopaminergic tone strongly predicts ultradian period.
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data in Figure 6 showing DA fluctuations that correlate with locomotor activity rhythms.

claim: Dopaminergic tone strongly predicts ultradian period.
source: We further reveal that striatal dopamine levels fluctuate in synchrony with ultradian activity cycles and that dopaminergic tone strongly predicts ultradian period.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis in Figure 6C showing correlation between mean DA concentration and period length.

claim: An arousal regulating, dopaminergic ultradian oscillator (DUO) operates in the mammalian brain.
source: Our data indicate that an arousal regulating, dopaminergic ultradian oscillator (DUO) operates in the mammalian brain, which normally cycles in harmony with the circadian clock, but can desynchronize when dopamine tone is elevated, thereby producing aberrant patterns of arousal which are strikingly similar to perturbed sleep-wake cycles comorbid with psychopathology.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the collective experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The DUO normally cycles in harmony with the circadian clock.
source: Our data indicate that an arousal regulating, dopaminergic ultradian oscillator (DUO) operates in the mammalian brain, which normally cycles in harmony with the circadian clock, but can desynchronize when dopamine tone is elevated, thereby producing aberrant patterns of arousal which are strikingly similar to perturbed sleep-wake cycles comorbid with psychopathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4 and Figure 7 showing coordinated rhythms in intact mice.

claim: The DUO can desynchronize when dopamine tone is elevated.
source: Our data indicate that an arousal regulating, dopaminergic ultradian oscillator (DUO) operates in the mammalian brain, which normally cycles in harmony with the circadian clock, but can desynchronize when dopamine tone is elevated, thereby producing aberrant patterns of arousal which are strikingly similar to perturbed sleep-wake cycles comorbid with psychopathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figures 7 and 9 showing dual-component rhythms in Slc6a3−/− and Meth-treated mice.

claim: DUO desynchronization produces aberrant patterns of arousal strikingly similar to perturbed sleep-wake cycles comorbid with psychopathology.
source: Our data indicate that an arousal regulating, dopaminergic ultradian oscillator (DUO) operates in the mammalian brain, which normally cycles in harmony with the circadian clock, but can desynchronize when dopamine tone is elevated, thereby producing aberrant patterns of arousal which are strikingly similar to perturbed sleep-wake cycles comorbid with psychopathology.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with literature on sleep-wake abnormalities in psychiatric conditions, discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: Ultradian rhythms with periods ranging from one to several hours have been linked to various aspects of mammalian physiology.
source: Ultradian rhythms with periods ranging from one to several hours have been linked to various aspects of mammalian physiology. Usually superimposed on the 24-hr diurnal or circadian rhythm, ultradian oscillations have been observed in the context of locomotion, sleep, feeding, body temperature, serum hormones, and brain monoamines in species ranging from fruit flies to humans (Tannenbaum and Martin, 1976; Ibuka et al., 1977; Rusak, 1977; Daan and Slopsema, 1978; Honma and Hiroshige, 1978; Dowse et al., 1987; Rivkees, 2003; van Oort et al., 2007; Dowse et al., 2010; Seki and Tanimura, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Ultradian oscillations have been observed in the context of locomotion, sleep, feeding, body temperature, serum hormones, and brain monoamines in species ranging from fruit flies to humans.
source: Usually superimposed on the 24-hr diurnal or circadian rhythm, ultradian oscillations have been observed in the context of locomotion, sleep, feeding, body temperature, serum hormones, and brain monoamines in species ranging from fruit flies to humans (Tannenbaum and Martin, 1976; Ibuka et al., 1977; Rusak, 1977; Daan and Slopsema, 1978; Honma and Hiroshige, 1978; Dowse et al., 1987; Rivkees, 2003; van Oort et al., 2007; Dowse et al., 2010; Seki and Tanimura, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Physiological cycles most frequently exhibit periods of 2–6 hr.
source: These physiological cycles most frequently exhibit periods of 2–6 hr, adopting harmonics of the 24-hr daily light–dark cycle or the endogenous circadian rhythm, when external timing cues are absent.
evidence: This is a general statement about ultradian rhythms based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The generation of ultradian rhythms does not depend on a functional circadian system nor a light:dark cycle.
source: However, the generation of such ultradian rhythms does not depend on a functional circadian system nor a light:dark cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by the following sentence citing studies in SCN-lesioned and clock-disrupted animals.

claim: Ultradian locomotor oscillations persist in rodents housed in constant darkness even upon ablation of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
source: Ultradian locomotor oscillations persist in rodents housed in constant darkness even upon ablation of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the site of the master circadian pacemaker (Ibuka et al., 1977; Rusak, 1977), or genetic disruption of the circadian clock (Vitaterna et al., 1994; Bunger et al., 2000) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and by data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Ultradian locomotor oscillations persist in rodents housed in constant darkness even upon genetic disruption of the circadian clock.
source: Ultradian locomotor oscillations persist in rodents housed in constant darkness even upon ablation of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the site of the master circadian pacemaker (Ibuka et al., 1977; Rusak, 1977), or genetic disruption of the circadian clock (Vitaterna et al., 1994; Bunger et al., 2000) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and by data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Ultradian activity cycles may not simply be driven by metabolic demand since the 2- to 3-hr rhythm in foraging activity observed in the common vole persists even in the absence of food.
source: These ultradian activity cycles may not simply be driven by metabolic demand since the 2- to 3-hr rhythm in foraging activity observed in the common vole persists even in the absence of food (Gerkema and van der Leest, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study in voles.

claim: One adaptive value of ultradian activity rhythms may lie in the facilitation of social synchrony, which is suggested to reduce predator risk in the common vole.
source: Studies in this species further indicate that one adaptive value of ultradian activity rhythms may lie in the facilitation of social synchrony, which is suggested to reduce predator risk in this species (Gerkema and Verhulst, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and involves speculation about adaptive value.

claim: Ultradian locomotor rhythms have received little research attention, likely owing to their frequently masked expression and unstable periodicity in contrast with circadian activity rhythms.
source: However, despite their prevalence and hypothesized biological significance, ultradian locomotor rhythms have received little research attention, likely owing to their frequently masked expression and unstable periodicity in contrast with circadian activity rhythms (Ruis et al., 1987; Schibler, 2008) (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1C,D showing period variability.

claim: Methamphetamine-induced rhythms of locomotor activity occur in the absence of a functional circadian clock.
source: In addition to ultradian oscillations, methamphetamine-induced rhythms of locomotor activity occur in the absence of a functional circadian clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by the subsequent citations to studies on methamphetamine-induced rhythms.

claim: When provided in the drinking water, methamphetamines (Meth) induce a daily activity bout in addition to the expected circadian rhythm.
source: When provided in the drinking water, methamphetamines (Meth) induce a daily activity bout in addition to the expected circadian rhythm (Honma et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Meth-dependent component is not abolished upon SCN lesion nor by genetic disruption of circadian clock function.
source: This Meth-dependent component—which typically adopts a period in the circadian range—is not abolished upon SCN lesion nor by genetic disruption of circadian clock function (Honma et al., 1987; Mohawk et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A methamphetamine-sensitive circadian oscillator (MASCO) outside the SCN exists which is capable of driving daily cycles of locomotor activity.
source: It was thus concluded that a methamphetamine-sensitive circadian oscillator (MASCO) outside the SCN exists which is capable of driving daily cycles of locomotor activity (Tataroglu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is based on a citation to prior work that proposed the MASCO concept.

claim: The cellular and molecular identity of the oscillator(s) driving ultradian and Meth-dependent rhythms is unknown.
source: Despite the longstanding recognition of ultradian and Meth-dependent rhythms, the underlying cellular and molecular identity of the oscillator(s) driving them is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Dopamine acts as both the principal oscillator output as well as an integral component of the DUO, determining oscillator period.
source: Our data suggest that dopamine acts as both the principal oscillator output as well as an integral component of the DUO, determining oscillator period.
evidence: This claim is based on the collective experimental findings showing DA fluctuations and period correlations.

claim: The previously described MASCO represents a long-period manifestation of the DUO resulting from elevated dopamine tone.
source: Our findings further indicate that the previously described MASCO represents a long-period manifestation of the DUO resulting from elevated dopamine tone.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing period lengthening with elevated DA tone.

claim: DUO, rather than circadian clock, dysregulation critically contributes to the sleep-wake abnormalities associated with psychopathology.
source: Importantly, our data support an intriguing proposition: that DUO, rather than circadian clock, dysregulation critically contributes to the sleep-wake abnormalities associated with psychopathology.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparison with clinical observations discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: Bmal1−/− mice exhibit ultradian activity rhythms with approximately 4-hr period in constant darkness.
source: Representative double-plotted actograms of running wheel activity in SCN-lesioned (SCNx) and Bmal1−/− mice in DD.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SCN-lesioned mice exhibit ultradian activity rhythms with approximately 4-hr period in constant darkness.
source: Representative double-plotted actograms of running wheel activity in SCN-lesioned (SCNx) and Bmal1−/− mice in DD.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There is no significant difference in locomotor period length between Bmal1−/− and SCN-lesioned mice in constant darkness.
source: Dot plot of locomotor period length in DD based on Lomb-Scargle periodogram analysis of seven consecutive days of activity recording (N = 65 for Bmal1−/− and N = 48 for SCNx; t111 = 0.2785, p = 0.78, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Locomotor activity is associated with an awakened state.
source: To gain insights into the mechanistic basis of ultradian locomotor rhythm generation, we considered that locomotor activity is associated with an awakened state (Welsh et al., 1988) and consequently, the ultradian locomotor rhythms observed in mice that lack circadian clock function (Figure 1) could be interpreted as rhythms of heightened wakefulness or arousal.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ultradian locomotor rhythms observed in mice that lack circadian clock function could be interpreted as rhythms of heightened wakefulness or arousal.
source: To gain insights into the mechanistic basis of ultradian locomotor rhythm generation, we considered that locomotor activity is associated with an awakened state (Welsh et al., 1988) and consequently, the ultradian locomotor rhythms observed in mice that lack circadian clock function (Figure 1) could be interpreted as rhythms of heightened wakefulness or arousal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the association between locomotor activity and arousal.

claim: A key role in arousal promotion has been attributed to distinct monoaminergic neuronal populations located in the upper brainstem and midbrain.
source: In mammals, a key role in arousal promotion has been attributed to distinct monoaminergic neuronal populations located in the upper brainstem and midbrain (Brown et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Altering extracellular levels of serotonin, norepinephrine, or histamine by genetic manipulation has only limited effects on locomotion.
source: While altering extracellular levels of the arousal-associated monoamines serotonin, norepinephrine, or histamine by genetic manipulation has only limited effects on locomotion (Thomas and Palmiter, 1997; Bengel et al., 1998; Xu et al., 2000; Parmentier et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2006), depleting the brain of dopamine (DA) profoundly abrogates locomotor activity (Zhou and Palmiter, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Depleting the brain of dopamine profoundly abrogates locomotor activity.
source: While altering extracellular levels of the arousal-associated monoamines serotonin, norepinephrine, or histamine by genetic manipulation has only limited effects on locomotion (Thomas and Palmiter, 1997; Bengel et al., 1998; Xu et al., 2000; Parmentier et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2006), depleting the brain of dopamine (DA) profoundly abrogates locomotor activity (Zhou and Palmiter, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Increasing extracellular DA levels induces hyperlocomotion.
source: Moreover, increasing extracellular DA levels induces hyperlocomotion (Giros et al., 1996) and lengthens the time spent awake (Wisor et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Increasing extracellular DA levels lengthens the time spent awake.
source: Moreover, increasing extracellular DA levels induces hyperlocomotion (Giros et al., 1996) and lengthens the time spent awake (Wisor et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Slc6a3−/− mice exhibit hyperdopaminergia due to the lack of DAT-mediated DA reuptake into dopaminergic neurons.
source: Slc6a3−/− mice exhibit hyperdopaminergia due to the lack of DAT-mediated DA reuptake into dopaminergic neurons, leading to a hyperactivity phenotype (Giros et al., 1996; Gainetdinov et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior characterization of the Slc6a3−/− mouse model.

claim: Slc6a3−/− mice exhibit a hyperactivity phenotype.
source: Slc6a3−/− mice exhibit hyperdopaminergia due to the lack of DAT-mediated DA reuptake into dopaminergic neurons, leading to a hyperactivity phenotype (Giros et al., 1996; Gainetdinov et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior characterization of the Slc6a3−/− mouse model.

claim: The presence of the circadian clock and/or a light:dark cycle frequently masks ultradian activity rhythms.
source: As the presence of the circadian clock and/or a light:dark cycle frequently masks ultradian activity rhythms (Schibler, 2008), we assessed the locomotor behavioral consequences of DAT elimination in the absence of the master SCN circadian pacemaker.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SCNx-Slc6a3−/− mice showed rhythms whose periods were three times longer than control mice.
source: While control mice (SCNx-Slc6a3+/+) exhibited ultradian activity rhythms with the expected ∼4-hr period, SCNx-Slc6a3−/− mice showed rhythms whose periods were three times longer (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Bmal1−/−, Slc6a3−/− mice exhibited approximately 12–14-hr rhythms in locomotor activity.
source: Bmal1−/−, Slc6a3−/− mice exhibited ∼12–14-hr rhythms in locomotor activity, largely phenocopying the SCNx-Slc6a3−/− mice, while their Bmal1−/−, Slc6a3+/+ littermates showed ∼4-hr periods as expected for isodopaminergic mice lacking circadian clock function (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Bmal1−/−, Slc6a3+/+ mice showed approximately 4-hr periods.
source: Bmal1−/−, Slc6a3−/− mice exhibited ∼12–14-hr rhythms in locomotor activity, largely phenocopying the SCNx-Slc6a3−/− mice, while their Bmal1−/−, Slc6a3+/+ littermates showed ∼4-hr periods as expected for isodopaminergic mice lacking circadian clock function (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: DAT removal markedly increases ultradian cycle length.
source: Together, these results suggest that DAT removal markedly increases ultradian cycle length.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the data from Figure 2.

claim: DAT-mediated DA uptake can be reversed by the selective action of the psychostimulant methamphetamine.
source: In order to corroborate that DAT removal indeed lengthens the period of the ultradian activity cycles, we took into account that DAT-mediated DA uptake can be reversed by the selective action of the psychostimulant methamphetamine (Meth) (Howell and Kimmel, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on methamphetamine's mechanism of action.

claim: Meth leads to increased extracellular DA concentrations as in the case of Slc6a3 gene disruption.
source: Because Meth leads to increased extracellular DA concentrations as in the case of Slc6a3 gene disruption, we speculated that Meth treatment would result in a, possibly gradual, period lengthening of the ultradian locomotor rhythms.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about methamphetamine's effects on DA levels.

claim: When treated with increasing concentrations of Meth via drinking water in DD, Bmal1−/− animals showed a gradual lengthening of the initial approximately 4-hr locomotor oscillations.
source: Indeed when we treated Bmal1−/− animals with increasing concentrations of Meth via drinking water in DD, we observed a gradual lengthening of the initial ∼4-hr locomotor oscillations and this was accompanied by a corresponding increase in activity bout length (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Meth treatment was accompanied by a corresponding increase in activity bout length.
source: Indeed when we treated Bmal1−/− animals with increasing concentrations of Meth via drinking water in DD, we observed a gradual lengthening of the initial ∼4-hr locomotor oscillations and this was accompanied by a corresponding increase in activity bout length (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The period increase in response to elevating Meth concentrations did not halt in the circadian range, rather, oscillations continued to lengthen with individual animals reaching periods of 100 hr or more.
source: Of note, the period increase in response to elevating Meth concentrations did not halt in the circadian range, rather, oscillations continued to lengthen with individual animals reaching periods of 100 hr or more (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Gradual period lengthening of ultradian locomotor rhythms was also observed in Bmal1−/− animals exposed to amphetamine.
source: Gradual period lengthening of ultradian locomotor rhythms was also observed in Bmal1−/− animals exposed to amphetamine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), a drug similarly targeting DAT (Howell and Kimmel, 2008), but with lower efficacy than Meth (Goodwin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B and citations about amphetamine's mechanism.

claim: Amphetamine is a drug similarly targeting DAT but with lower efficacy than Meth.
source: Gradual period lengthening of ultradian locomotor rhythms was also observed in Bmal1−/− animals exposed to amphetamine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), a drug similarly targeting DAT (Howell and Kimmel, 2008), but with lower efficacy than Meth (Goodwin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on amphetamine's mechanism and efficacy.

claim: DAT targeting psychostimulants affect an endogenous ultradian rhythm generator by increasing period length.
source: These results argue that DAT targeting psychostimulants affect an endogenous ultradian rhythm generator by increasing period length.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the methamphetamine and amphetamine data.

claim: Subcutaneously implanted osmotic minipumps that continuously infused Meth over a period of 2 weeks resulted in significant ultradian period lengthening in Bmal1−/− animals.
source: To address this possibility, we subcutaneously implanted Bmal1−/− mice with osmotic minipumps that continuously infused Meth over a period of 2 weeks. Running wheel analysis in DD of Meth-infused Bmal1−/− animals demonstrated a significant ultradian period lengthening upon drug infusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D) suggesting that rhythmic uptake is not required for Meth to exert its period lengthening effect, in line with a previous study performed in rats (Honma et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Rhythmic uptake is not required for Meth to exert its period lengthening effect.
source: Running wheel analysis in DD of Meth-infused Bmal1−/− animals demonstrated a significant ultradian period lengthening upon drug infusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D) suggesting that rhythmic uptake is not required for Meth to exert its period lengthening effect, in line with a previous study performed in rats (Honma et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is based on the continuous infusion experiment and supported by a citation.

claim: The long-period oscillations observed in Meth-treated animals, and likewise in Slc6a3−/− mice, are due to period expansion of an endogenous ultradian rhythm of arousal.
source: Together, these findings support the notion that the long-period oscillations observed in Meth-treated animals, and likewise in Slc6a3−/− mice, are due to period expansion of an endogenous ultradian rhythm of arousal.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Running wheel activity data from intact mice often do not provide strong indications of ultradian activity rhythms.
source: Indeed, running wheel activity data from intact mice often do not provide strong indications of ultradian activity rhythms.
evidence: This is a general observation about the difficulty of detecting ultradian rhythms in intact mice.

claim: When ambulatory behavior was recorded using telemetry, three evenly spaced activity bouts during the active (night) phase were frequently detected.
source: However, when we recorded ambulatory behavior using telemetry, we frequently detected three, evenly spaced activity bouts during the active (night) phase (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The observed approximately 4 hr peak-to-peak spacing is in line with a previous study on several circadian competent mouse strains where ultradian rhythms with similar period length were detected.
source: The observed ∼4 hr peak-to-peak spacing is in line with a previous study on several circadian competent mouse strains where ultradian rhythms with similar period length were detected (Dowse et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The absence of a clearly discernable approximately 4-hr rhythmic component during the light portion of the daily LD cycle is likely due to masking by the SCN and/or light.
source: The absence of a clearly discernable ∼4-hr rhythmic component during the light portion of the daily LD cycle (Figure 4A) is likely due to masking by the SCN and/or light.
evidence: This is an inference based on known masking effects of the SCN and light.

claim: Slc6a3−/− mice never showed a triple-peak activity pattern at night.
source: Unlike WT mice, Slc6a3−/− mice never showed a triple-peak activity pattern at night (Figure 4B), and spectral density analysis in the ultradian (2–8 hr) range (Figure 4C) underscores that rhythm generation is significantly altered in these animals while total daily activity is not (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Rhythm generation is significantly altered in Slc6a3−/− mice while total daily activity is not.
source: Unlike WT mice, Slc6a3−/− mice never showed a triple-peak activity pattern at night (Figure 4B), and spectral density analysis in the ultradian (2–8 hr) range (Figure 4C) underscores that rhythm generation is significantly altered in these animals while total daily activity is not (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: When C57BL/6 mice carrying a telemetry implant were provided with Meth in their drinking water, a gradual lengthening of the interval between the night-time activity peaks was observed.
source: When we provided C57BL/6 mice carrying a telemetry implant with Meth in their drinking water, we observed a gradual lengthening of the interval between the night-time activity peaks (Figure 4F,G), resulting in the transformation of the triple peak (Figure 4G, white trace and white triangles) into a dual or single night-time activity peak pattern at the highest (100 mg/l) Meth concentration (Figure 4G, black trace and black triangles).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: The triple peak night-time activity pattern transformed into a dual or single night-time activity peak pattern at the highest (100 mg/l) Meth concentration.
source: When we provided C57BL/6 mice carrying a telemetry implant with Meth in their drinking water, we observed a gradual lengthening of the interval between the night-time activity peaks (Figure 4F,G), resulting in the transformation of the triple peak (Figure 4G, white trace and white triangles) into a dual or single night-time activity peak pattern at the highest (100 mg/l) Meth concentration (Figure 4G, black trace and black triangles).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Spectral density analysis revealed a marked reduction in ultradian frequencies upon Meth treatment.
source: This was corroborated by spectral density analysis revealing a marked reduction in ultradian frequencies upon Meth treatment (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Blocking DA reuptake lengthens ultradian activity bout intervals in circadian competent mice.
source: Together, these results indicate that blocking DA reuptake also lengthens ultradian activity bout intervals in circadian competent mice, arguing that an ultradian oscillator is not 'activated' by circadian disruption, but rather continuously operative alongside the circadian timer.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the data from Figure 4.

claim: An ultradian oscillator is not 'activated' by circadian disruption, but rather continuously operative alongside the circadian timer.
source: Together, these results indicate that blocking DA reuptake also lengthens ultradian activity bout intervals in circadian competent mice, arguing that an ultradian oscillator is not 'activated' by circadian disruption, but rather continuously operative alongside the circadian timer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of ultradian rhythms in both intact and circadian-disrupted mice.

claim: Prolonged Meth-treatment in intact WT mice can lead to profound period lengthening of ultradian rhythms, often into the circabidian (48 hr) range.
source: As with Bmal1−/− mice, prolonged Meth-treatment in intact WT mice can lead to profound period lengthening of ultradian rhythms, often into the circabidian (48 hr) range (for examples see Figures 5E, 7F, 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5E, 7F, 9B.

claim: Manipulations aimed at lowering DA tone should lead to period shortening.
source: Given that both DAT disruption and Meth treatment elevate extracellular DA and concurrently lengthen ultradian rhythm period, we speculated that manipulations aimed at lowering DA tone should conversely lead to period shortening.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed relationship between DA tone and period length.

claim: Hal selectively blocks the DA receptor D2 (DRD2).
source: Hal selectively blocks the DA receptor D2 (DRD2) (Strange, 2008), which is expressed on postsynaptic target sites of DA neuronal projections but also presynaptically as an autoreceptor (Schmitz et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on haloperidol's mechanism.

claim: DRD2 is expressed on postsynaptic target sites of DA neuronal projections and also presynaptically as an autoreceptor.
source: Hal selectively blocks the DA receptor D2 (DRD2) (Strange, 2008), which is expressed on postsynaptic target sites of DA neuronal projections but also presynaptically as an autoreceptor (Schmitz et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When given chronically, Hal has been reported to electrically silence midbrain DA neurons.
source: Importantly, when given chronically as in our case, Hal has been reported to electrically silence midbrain DA neurons (White and Wang, 1983) and to markedly lower extracellular DA levels in the striatum/nucleus accumbens regions in rats (Lane and Blaha, 1987; Ichikawa and Meltzer, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When given chronically, Hal markedly lowers extracellular DA levels in the striatum/nucleus accumbens regions in rats.
source: Importantly, when given chronically as in our case, Hal has been reported to electrically silence midbrain DA neurons (White and Wang, 1983) and to markedly lower extracellular DA levels in the striatum/nucleus accumbens regions in rats (Lane and Blaha, 1987; Ichikawa and Meltzer, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bmal1−/− mice responded with successive locomotor period shortening to increasing concentrations of Hal.
source: As predicted, Bmal1−/− mice responded with successive locomotor period shortening to increasing concentrations of Hal (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Hal-mediated shortening of the long-period behavioral rhythms was observed in Bmal1−/− and wild-type mice treated concurrently with Meth.
source: We also observed Hal-mediated shortening of the long-period behavioral rhythms in Bmal1−/− and wild-type mice treated concurrently with Meth (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C–F.

claim: A period shortening effect of Hal could be discerned from the core body temperature fluctuations of Slc6a3−/− mice, which increased in frequency.
source: A period shortening effect of Hal could also be discerned from the core body temperature fluctuations of Slc6a3−/− mice, which increased in frequency (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The temperature response to Hal was concentration dependent and spectral density analysis confirmed a successive increase of the ultradian component upon Hal exposure.
source: This response, which mirrored the locomotor behavioral response (not shown), was concentration dependent and spectral density analysis confirmed a successive increase of the ultradian component upon Hal exposure (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The ultradian rhythms observed in wildtype and Bmal1−/− mice and the long-period rhythms previously attributed to the MASCO are driven by the exact same oscillatory mechanism.
source: Together, these data strongly support the hypothesis that both the ultradian rhythms observed in wildtype and Bmal1−/− mice and the long-period rhythms previously attributed to the MASCO are driven by the exact same oscillatory mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective experimental findings showing bidirectional period modulation.

claim: Extracellular DA must oscillate in synchrony with the observed activity rhythms.
source: Given that DA is known to mediate arousal/wakefulness (Brown et al., 2012), it appears plausible that DA also serves as principal oscillator output, driving rhythms in arousal. We thus hypothesized that extracellular DA must oscillate in synchrony with the observed activity rhythms.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on DA's known role in arousal and the observed activity rhythms.

claim: Extracellular DA levels fluctuated concordantly with the activity cycles in Bmal1−/− mice.
source: The animals showed the expected short period rhythms in locomotor activity throughout the experiment (Figure 6A), and analysis of dialysates revealed that extracellular DA levels fluctuated concordantly with the activity cycles (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, compare solid red and black traces).
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The goodness of fit between the cosinor and the DA profiles indicated by the sum of squared errors suggests that the dialysate sampling procedure itself did not perturb the generation of the endogenous ultradian activity cycles.
source: The goodness of fit between the cosinor and the DA profiles indicated by the sum of squared errors (SSE = 0.050 ± 0.027, mean ± SEM, N = 7) suggests that the dialysate sampling procedure itself did not perturb the generation of the endogenous ultradian activity cycles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of the fit between DA and activity data.

claim: On average, only 3.2 ± 1.7% of 100,000 permutated DA profiles correlated as well or better than the experimentally observed DA measurements.
source: To determine the statistical significance of the observed agreement between the cosinor and the DA trace, we randomly permutated the individual time points of the DA trace and determined the percentage of permutated traces with an equal or better fit to the cosinor in comparison to the observed DA fluctuation. On average, only 3.2 ± 1.7% of 100,000 permutated DA profiles correlated as well or better than the experimentally observed DA measurements (Figure 6B), confirming that extracellular DA fluctuates in synchrony with the ultradian activity cycles.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Extracellular DA fluctuates in synchrony with the ultradian activity cycles.
source: On average, only 3.2 ± 1.7% of 100,000 permutated DA profiles correlated as well or better than the experimentally observed DA measurements (Figure 6B), confirming that extracellular DA fluctuates in synchrony with the ultradian activity cycles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the false discovery rate analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Linear regression revealed a highly significant correlation between mean DA concentration in the dialysate and ultradian locomotor period in Bmal1−/− animals.
source: Of particular note, linear regression revealed a highly significant correlation between mean DA concentration in the dialysate and ultradian locomotor period in the Bmal1−/− animals we tested (Figure 6C), which again supports a role of (extracellular) DA as a period determinant of the ultradian activity cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Extracellular DA is a period determinant of the ultradian activity cycle.
source: Of particular note, linear regression revealed a highly significant correlation between mean DA concentration in the dialysate and ultradian locomotor period in the Bmal1−/− animals we tested (Figure 6C), which again supports a role of (extracellular) DA as a period determinant of the ultradian activity cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between DA levels and period length.

claim: Significantly higher levels of DA and DOPAC were detected in tissue extracts of the CPu during the animal's active phase.
source: We detected significantly higher levels of DA as well as its immediate metabolite, 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid (DOPAC), in tissue extracts of the CPu during the animal's active phase (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was a significant increase in DOPAC levels and a trend towards elevated DA (p = 0.066) during the active period in the NAcc.
source: There was also a significant increase in DOPAC levels and a trend towards elevated DA (p = 0.066) during the active period in the NAcc, while extracts from the midbrain region, which contains the cell bodies of the striatal dopaminergic afferents, exhibited no detectable change (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Extracts from the midbrain region exhibited no detectable change in DA or DOPAC between active and inactive phases.
source: There was also a significant increase in DOPAC levels and a trend towards elevated DA (p = 0.066) during the active period in the NAcc, while extracts from the midbrain region, which contains the cell bodies of the striatal dopaminergic afferents, exhibited no detectable change (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was a significant correlation between locomotor period and DA content in CPu and midbrain punches collected during the active phase.
source: We also found a significant correlation between locomotor period and DA content in CPu and midbrain punches collected during the active phase (Figure 6E), again consistent with a role for DA as a period determinant of ultradian oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Under LD conditions, more fragmented daily activity was observed in Slc6a3−/− than their wildtype counterparts.
source: Under LD conditions, we observed more fragmented daily activity in Slc6a3−/− than their wildtype counterpars (Figure 7A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A,D.

claim: Upon release into constant darkness (DD), wild-type animals exhibited a daily rhythm with a period slightly shorter than 24 hr.
source: Upon release into constant darkness (DD), wild-type animals exhibited a daily rhythm with a period slightly shorter than 24 hr as expected for mice (Bunger et al., 2000) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and a citation.

claim: Slc6a3−/− mice repeatedly exhibited an additional activity component with periods longer than 24 hr in DD.
source: While this principal locomotor component was also observed in Slc6a3−/− mice, they repeatedly exhibited an additional activity component with periods longer than 24 hr (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D–F.

claim: The additional activity component in Slc6a3−/− mice was more evident after the first few weeks in DD.
source: This component, which was more evident after the first few weeks in DD, extended from the main activity component and lasted for several cycles before disappearing late in the subjective day (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There was no significant difference in the total amount of daily activity between Slc6a3−/− and wildtype mice even though the temporal pattern of locomotion is severely altered.
source: Overall, there was no significant difference in the total amount of daily activity even though the temporal pattern of locomotion in these mice is severely altered (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The observed dual component activity pattern in Slc6a3−/− mice shows striking similarities to the activity patterns of Meth-treated C57BL/6 mice.
source: The observed dual component activity pattern shows striking similarities to the activity patterns of Meth-treated C57BL/6 mice (Figure 7G–I), suggesting that the second rhythmic component is generated by the dopaminergic oscillator.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7G–I.

claim: The second rhythmic component in Slc6a3−/− mice is generated by the dopaminergic oscillator.
source: The observed dual component activity pattern shows striking similarities to the activity patterns of Meth-treated C57BL/6 mice (Figure 7G–I), suggesting that the second rhythmic component is generated by the dopaminergic oscillator.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between Slc6a3−/− and Meth-treated mice.

claim: A dual component activity pattern with two components oscillating at different frequencies has been observed in rats housed under a 22-hr LD cycle and attributed to a dissociation of molecular rhythms between the dorsal and ventral SCN.
source: However, such locomotor activity pattern, with two components oscillating at different frequencies, has also been observed in rats housed under a 22-hr LD cycle and have been attributed to a dissociation of molecular rhythms between the dorsal and ventral SCN (de la Iglesia et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In situ hybridization directed against Period1 transcripts did not indicate rhythmic desynchrony between or within SCN hemispheres in Slc6a3−/− mice.
source: In situ hybridization directed against Period1 transcripts did not indicate rhythmic desynchrony between or within SCN hemispheres. The riboprobe showed strong, homogenous staining throughout the SCN in the early subjective day, whereas little to no signal was detectable in the early subjective night, suggesting that SCN pacemaker function is unperturbed in Slc6a3−/− mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SCN pacemaker function is unperturbed in Slc6a3−/− mice.
source: The riboprobe showed strong, homogenous staining throughout the SCN in the early subjective day, whereas little to no signal was detectable in the early subjective night, suggesting that SCN pacemaker function is unperturbed in Slc6a3−/− mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the normal Per1 expression pattern in the SCN.

claim: The second rhythmic component of Slc6a3−/− mice is a product of the dopaminergic oscillator.
source: Together, these findings thus argue that the second rhythmic component of Slc6a3−/− mice is indeed a product of the above described dopaminergic oscillator.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the SCN analysis and behavioral data.

claim: DA neurons of the SN/VTA are by and large the exclusive source of striatal and midbrain DA.
source: Since striatal and midbrain DA levels vary concordantly with activity rhythms in Bmal1−/− mice, and DA neurons of the SN/VTA are by and large the exclusive source of striatal and midbrain DA, these neurons are a likely site of ultradian rhythm regulation, if not generation.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge about dopaminergic projections.

claim: DA neurons of the SN/VTA are a likely site of ultradian rhythm regulation, if not generation.
source: Since striatal and midbrain DA levels vary concordantly with activity rhythms in Bmal1−/− mice, and DA neurons of the SN/VTA are by and large the exclusive source of striatal and midbrain DA, these neurons are a likely site of ultradian rhythm regulation, if not generation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DA fluctuation data and anatomical knowledge.

claim: CNO stimulation of successfully transduced DAT-Cre mice evokes vigorous firing of dopamine neurons.
source: As augmenting firing frequency in DA neurons enhances DA release (Sulzer, 2011), and CNO stimulation of successfully transduced DAT-Cre mice evokes vigorous firing of dopamine neurons (Wang et al., 2013), CNO is expected to increase DA release.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Augmenting firing frequency in DA neurons enhances DA release.
source: As augmenting firing frequency in DA neurons enhances DA release (Sulzer, 2011), and CNO stimulation of successfully transduced DAT-Cre mice evokes vigorous firing of dopamine neurons (Wang et al., 2013), CNO is expected to increase DA release.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: I.p.-injection of CNO elevated extracellular DA in the striatum of AAV-hM3Dq transduced DAT-Cre mice and led to a prolonged increase in locomotor activity.
source: Consistently, i.p.-injection of CNO elevated extracellular DA in the striatum of those mice and led to a prolonged increase in locomotor activity (Figure 8C,D), which was absent in vehicle injected animals (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: 92.9 ± 5.1% and 87.8 ± 6.0% of the midbrain TH+ neurons also expressed the mCherry fusion tag in responsive DAT-Cre, SCNX and DAT-Cre, Bmal−/− mice, respectively.
source: Cell counting revealed that, 92.9 ± 5.1% and 87.8 ± 6.0% (mean ± SEM, N = 6 for both groups) of the midbrain TH+ neurons also expressed the mCherry fusion tag in responsive DAT-Cre, SCNX and DAT-Cre, Bmal−/− mice, respectively, confirming effective Cre-mediated hM3Dq expression in midbrain DA neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell counting data.

claim: Upon switching to CNO-containing drinking water, both AAV-hM3Dq transduced DAT-Cre, SCNx and DAT-Cre, Bmal1−/− mice responded with locomotor period lengthening.
source: Running wheel activity monitoring of virus-injected mice showed the expected short period locomotor oscillations, however, upon switching to CNO-containing drinking water (red arrows), both, AAV-hM3Dq transduced DAT-Cre, SCNx and DAT-Cre, Bmal1−/− mice responded with locomotor period lengthening (Figure 8E–H), an effect that was reversed when mice were returned to pure water (Figure 8G, blue arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8E–H.

claim: The period lengthening effect was reversed when mice were returned to pure water.
source: Running wheel activity monitoring of virus-injected mice showed the expected short period locomotor oscillations, however, upon switching to CNO-containing drinking water (red arrows), both, AAV-hM3Dq transduced DAT-Cre, SCNx and DAT-Cre, Bmal1−/− mice responded with locomotor period lengthening (Figure 8E–H), an effect that was reversed when mice were returned to pure water (Figure 8G, blue arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: A period lengthening was not observable in AAV-hM3Dq injected DAT-Cre0/0, Bmal1−/− mice upon CNO exposure.
source: As expected, a period lengthening was not observable in AAV-hM3Dq injected DAT-Cre0/0, Bmal1−/− mice upon CNO exposure (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by control data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Elevating DA tone by selective excitation of DA neurons lengthens ultradian locomotor period.
source: These results further corroborate that elevating DA tone, in this case by selective excitation of DA neurons, lengthens ultradian locomotor period and that the oscillator driving ultradian rhythmicity comprises DA neurons of the VTA/SN region.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the chemogenetic activation data.

claim: The oscillator driving ultradian rhythmicity comprises DA neurons of the VTA/SN region.
source: These results further corroborate that elevating DA tone, in this case by selective excitation of DA neurons, lengthens ultradian locomotor period and that the oscillator driving ultradian rhythmicity comprises DA neurons of the VTA/SN region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemogenetic activation data.

claim: Under normal conditions, the DUO cycles in harmony with the circadian SCN pacemaker.
source: Collectively, our results provide strong evidence that a dopaminergic ultradian oscillator (DUO) driving rhythms of behavioral arousal is continuously operative in the mammalian brain. We propose that under normal conditions, this DUO cycles in harmony with the circadian SCN pacemaker and that the rhythmic information of both the SCN and the DUO are integrated at a common downstream site to create the daily pattern in locomotor activity (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: The rhythmic information of both the SCN and the DUO are integrated at a common downstream site to create the daily pattern in locomotor activity.
source: We propose that under normal conditions, this DUO cycles in harmony with the circadian SCN pacemaker and that the rhythmic information of both the SCN and the DUO are integrated at a common downstream site to create the daily pattern in locomotor activity (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Elevation of DA tone can lead to DUO period lengthening, which either results in DUO free-run or reinstatement of oscillator synchrony albeit at a different harmonic.
source: However, elevation of DA tone can lead to DUO period lengthening, which either results in DUO free-run (for example, Figure 7D,G) or reinstatement of oscillator synchrony albeit at a different harmonic (Figure 9B, e.g., 48 hr).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental observations in Slc6a3−/− and Meth-treated mice.

claim: The DUO appears as a highly tunable oscillator, able to adopt period lengths from a few hours to multiple days.
source: The DUO appears as a highly tunable oscillator, able to adopt period lengths from a few hours to multiple days.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the range of periods observed across experiments.

claim: The circadian timer cannot adopt periods that are more than a few hours off from 24 hr when its limits of entrainment are tested experimentally.
source: This is in stark contrast to the circadian timer which cannot adopt periods that are more than a few hours off from 24 hr when its limits of entrainment are tested experimentally (Aschoff and Pohl, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on circadian entrainment limits.

claim: DA acts as an output of the DUO.
source: Given that DA is known to stimulate locomotor activity (Zhou and Palmiter, 1995), our observation of a cyclical rise in extracellular striatal DA, which is in synchrony with ultradian activity rhythms, argues that DA acts as an output of the DUO.
evidence: This is an inference based on DA's known effects on locomotion and the observed DA fluctuations.

claim: DA is an integral component of the oscillatory mechanism itself.
source: Our finding that manipulations affecting extracellular DA levels alter oscillator period and that extracellular DA tone shows a remarkably high correlation with activity cycle length, strongly suggests that DA is a period determinant and therefore must be an integral component of the oscillatory mechanism itself.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between DA levels and period length.

claim: All period-altering manipulations directly impinge upon DA neuronal physiology.
source: As all period-altering manipulations directly impinge upon DA neuronal physiology, this suggests that either (i) DA neurons are the site of ultradian rhythm generation or (ii) they are a key cog in the oscillatory mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the experimental manipulations used in the study.

claim: Either DA neurons are the site of ultradian rhythm generation or they are a key cog in the oscillatory mechanism.
source: As all period-altering manipulations directly impinge upon DA neuronal physiology, this suggests that either (i) DA neurons are the site of ultradian rhythm generation or (ii) they are a key cog in the oscillatory mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The chemogenetic activation experiments indicate that the relevant DA neuronal population is located in the midbrain.
source: The chemogenetic activation experiments indicate that the relevant DA neuronal population is located in the midbrain as selective activation of DA neurons in this region had a period lengthening effect on the ultradian activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemogenetic activation data in Figure 8.

claim: The circadian and ultradian locomotor rhythms are normally harmonized.
source: Our data indicate that the circadian and ultradian locomotor rhythms are normally harmonized (for instance, Figure 9A), suggesting that the circadian pacemaker and the DUO interact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of coordinated rhythms in intact mice.

claim: The circadian pacemaker and the DUO interact.
source: Our data indicate that the circadian and ultradian locomotor rhythms are normally harmonized (for instance, Figure 9A), suggesting that the circadian pacemaker and the DUO interact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the harmonization of rhythms.

claim: Extracellular DA was reported to fluctuate diurnally in the rodent striatum.
source: Of note, extracellular DA was reported to fluctuate diurnally in the rodent striatum (Hood et al., 2010), which was abrogated in Slc6a3−/− mice (Gallardo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Diurnal DA fluctuation was abrogated in Slc6a3−/− mice.
source: Of note, extracellular DA was reported to fluctuate diurnally in the rodent striatum (Hood et al., 2010), which was abrogated in Slc6a3−/− mice (Gallardo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dopamine content in whole brain extracts from circadian-intact rats kept under LD showed a strong ultradian variation with no obvious evidence for a diurnal rhythmic component.
source: Note however, that dopamine content in whole brain extracts from circadian-intact rats kept under LD showed a strong ultradian variation with no obvious evidence for a diurnal rhythmic component (Scheving et al., 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Microdialysis did not reveal a day:night difference in extracellular DA levels in the striatal NAcc region when measured in DD.
source: Also, microdialysis did not reveal a day:night difference in extracellular DA levels in the striatal NAcc region when measured in DD (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mice lacking clock gene Rev-erbα exhibit elevated DA levels and hyperactivity.
source: This same study reported elevated DA levels and hyperactivity in mice lacking clock gene Rev-erbα, suggesting that the circadian clock, possibly intrinsic to DA neurons themselves, has a role in DA regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The circadian clock, possibly intrinsic to DA neurons themselves, has a role in DA regulation.
source: This same study reported elevated DA levels and hyperactivity in mice lacking clock gene Rev-erbα, suggesting that the circadian clock, possibly intrinsic to DA neurons themselves, has a role in DA regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study on Rev-erbα knockout mice.

claim: Knockdown of the core circadian clock component Clock in DA neurons of the murine VTA increases electrical firing rate in VTA neurons and enhances locomotor response to novel objects.
source: Indeed, knockdown of the core circadian clock component Clock in DA neurons of the murine VTA, increases electrical firing rate in VTA neurons and enhances locomotor response to novel objects (Mukherjee et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There were no systematic differences in ultradian locomotor period between SCNx and Bmal1−/− mice in constant darkness conditions, regardless of DAT status.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe any systematic differences in ultradian locomotor period between SCNx and Bmal1−/− mice in constant darkness conditions, regardless of DAT status (Figures 1, 2), suggesting that extra-SCN circadian clocks have no role in DUO-mediated ultradian locomotor rhythm generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Extra-SCN circadian clocks have no role in DUO-mediated ultradian locomotor rhythm generation.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe any systematic differences in ultradian locomotor period between SCNx and Bmal1−/− mice in constant darkness conditions, regardless of DAT status (Figures 1, 2), suggesting that extra-SCN circadian clocks have no role in DUO-mediated ultradian locomotor rhythm generation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of difference between SCNx and Bmal1−/− mice.

claim: The postulated MASCO represents a long-period manifestation of the DUO as a result of methamphetamine's action on the dopamine transporter.
source: Our data also provide evidence that the postulated MASCO (Tataroglu et al., 2006) represents a long-period manifestation of the DUO as a result of methamphetamine's action on the dopamine transporter, blocking dopamine reuptake thereby increasing extracellular DA levels.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the methamphetamine experiments.

claim: The dopamine system has been implicated with the food-entrainable oscillator (FEO).
source: Interestingly, the dopamine system has been also implicated with another behavioral timing system: the food-entrainable oscillator (FEO).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work linking dopamine to the FEO.

claim: The FEO is a circadian independent oscillator.
source: This circadian independent oscillator (Pitts et al., 2003; Pendergast et al., 2009; Storch and Weitz, 2009) drives food-anticipatory locomotor activity (FAA) that emerges when food access is restricted to a few hours each day (Mistlberger, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the FEO.

claim: D1 (DRD1) and D2 (DRD2) receptor antagonists attenuate FAA additively.
source: D1 (DRD1) and D2 (DRD2) receptor antagonists attenuate FAA additively (Liu et al., 2012) while pharmacological DRD2, but not DRD1, activation altered the phase of FAA (Smit et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pharmacological DRD2, but not DRD1, activation altered the phase of FAA.
source: D1 (DRD1) and D2 (DRD2) receptor antagonists attenuate FAA additively (Liu et al., 2012) while pharmacological DRD2, but not DRD1, activation altered the phase of FAA (Smit et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DRD1 but not DRD2 is necessary for the appropriate expression of FAA.
source: Most recently, using knockout mice, it was revealed that DRD1 but not DRD2 is necessary for the appropriate expression of FAA and that rescuing dopamine signaling selectively within the dorsal striatum was sufficient to restore FAA in dopamine-deficient mice (Gallardo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rescuing dopamine signaling selectively within the dorsal striatum was sufficient to restore FAA in dopamine-deficient mice.
source: Most recently, using knockout mice, it was revealed that DRD1 but not DRD2 is necessary for the appropriate expression of FAA and that rescuing dopamine signaling selectively within the dorsal striatum was sufficient to restore FAA in dopamine-deficient mice (Gallardo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dopamine signaling affects food intake as mice lacking dopamine are lethargic and do not actively consume food.
source: While these findings argue that food cues engage the dopamine system to alter daily locomotor activity patterns, it is clear that dopamine signaling also affects food intake as mice lacking dopamine are lethargic and do not actively consume food (Zhou and Palmiter, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The DUO is a universal driver of ultradian behavioral rhythms in mammals.
source: Considering that the DUO is a universal driver of ultradian behavioral rhythms in mammals, the finding that ultradian bouts of running-wheel and feeding activity are co-expressed in the common vole (van der Veen et al., 2006) suggests that dopamine can synchronously drive food seeking and general activity, which is in line with the view that dopamine acts as a general promoter of motivated arousal.
evidence: This is a claim about the generality of the DUO based on the study's findings.

claim: Ultradian bouts of running-wheel and feeding activity are co-expressed in the common vole.
source: Considering that the DUO is a universal driver of ultradian behavioral rhythms in mammals, the finding that ultradian bouts of running-wheel and feeding activity are co-expressed in the common vole (van der Veen et al., 2006) suggests that dopamine can synchronously drive food seeking and general activity, which is in line with the view that dopamine acts as a general promoter of motivated arousal.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dopamine can synchronously drive food seeking and general activity.
source: Considering that the DUO is a universal driver of ultradian behavioral rhythms in mammals, the finding that ultradian bouts of running-wheel and feeding activity are co-expressed in the common vole (van der Veen et al., 2006) suggests that dopamine can synchronously drive food seeking and general activity, which is in line with the view that dopamine acts as a general promoter of motivated arousal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-expression of feeding and activity rhythms and the role of the DUO.

claim: Dopamine acts as a general promoter of motivated arousal.
source: Considering that the DUO is a universal driver of ultradian behavioral rhythms in mammals, the finding that ultradian bouts of running-wheel and feeding activity are co-expressed in the common vole (van der Veen et al., 2006) suggests that dopamine can synchronously drive food seeking and general activity, which is in line with the view that dopamine acts as a general promoter of motivated arousal.
evidence: This is a general statement about dopamine's role supported by the experimental findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Slc6a3−/− mice have been proposed as a model for schizophrenia.
source: Slc6a3−/− mice have been proposed as a model for schizophrenia (Gainetdinov et al., 2001) and the DA hypothesis of schizophrenia states that DA elevation is causal to the behavioral symptoms of this psychiatric condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The DA hypothesis of schizophrenia states that DA elevation is causal to the behavioral symptoms of this psychiatric condition.
source: Slc6a3−/− mice have been proposed as a model for schizophrenia (Gainetdinov et al., 2001) and the DA hypothesis of schizophrenia states that DA elevation is causal to the behavioral symptoms of this psychiatric condition.
evidence: This is a statement about the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia.

claim: Circabidian (48 hr) or free-running rhythms in locomotor activity have been observed in schizophrenic subjects.
source: Intriguingly, circabidian (48 hr) or free-running rhythms in locomotor activity reminiscent of the behavioral patterns we detected in Slc6a3−/− or Meth-treated mice (Figures 4F, 7C,F, 9B) have been observed in schizophrenic subjects (Wirz-Justice et al., 2001; Wulff et al., 2012), suggesting that DUO dysregulation underlies the rest-activity aberrations associated with schizophrenia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: DUO dysregulation underlies the rest-activity aberrations associated with schizophrenia.
source: Intriguingly, circabidian (48 hr) or free-running rhythms in locomotor activity reminiscent of the behavioral patterns we detected in Slc6a3−/− or Meth-treated mice (Figures 4F, 7C,F, 9B) have been observed in schizophrenic subjects (Wirz-Justice et al., 2001; Wulff et al., 2012), suggesting that DUO dysregulation underlies the rest-activity aberrations associated with schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the similarity between mouse and human behavioral patterns.

claim: Actigraphy recordings in schizophrenic patients revealed that Hal treatment reduces circadian/diurnal locomotor amplitude and leads to the emergence of ultradian activity bouts.
source: Furthermore, actigraphy recordings in schizophrenic patients also revealed that Hal treatment reduces circadian/diurnal locomotor amplitude and leads to the emergence of ultradian activity bouts (Wirz-Justice et al., 1997, 2009), effects we likewise observed in Slc6a3−/− mice in response to Hal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Transient DUO period lengthening might account for the rest-activity pattern abnormalities observed during manic episodes in bipolar disorder.
source: Transient DUO period lengthening might equally account for the rest-activity pattern abnormalities observed during manic episodes in bipolar disorder, which has been also associated with altered DA tone (Berk et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the association between bipolar disorder and altered DA tone.

claim: Bipolar disorder has been associated with altered DA tone.
source: Transient DUO period lengthening might equally account for the rest-activity pattern abnormalities observed during manic episodes in bipolar disorder, which has been also associated with altered DA tone (Berk et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Bipolar subjects have been reported to show rapid, 48-hr cycling between mania and depression.
source: Bipolar subjects have been reported to show rapid, 48-hr cycling between mania and depression (Gann et al., 1993; Wilk and Hegerl, 2010), one to multiple 48-hr sleep–wake cycles when switching from depression to mania (Wehr et al., 1982), or a long-period 'free-running' rhythm of wakefulness (Wehr et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Bipolar subjects show one to multiple 48-hr sleep–wake cycles when switching from depression to mania.
source: Bipolar subjects have been reported to show rapid, 48-hr cycling between mania and depression (Gann et al., 1993; Wilk and Hegerl, 2010), one to multiple 48-hr sleep–wake cycles when switching from depression to mania (Wehr et al., 1982), or a long-period 'free-running' rhythm of wakefulness (Wehr et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior clinical studies.

claim: Bipolar subjects show a long-period 'free-running' rhythm of wakefulness.
source: Bipolar subjects have been reported to show rapid, 48-hr cycling between mania and depression (Gann et al., 1993; Wilk and Hegerl, 2010), one to multiple 48-hr sleep–wake cycles when switching from depression to mania (Wehr et al., 1982), or a long-period 'free-running' rhythm of wakefulness (Wehr et al., 1998).
